extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining inventorship and for construing claim terms during patent examination (BRI, plain meaning, lexicography, disavowal, means‑plus‑function, and preamble effect). Primarily directed at examiners but also informative for applicants and practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventorship under 35 U.S.C. 116
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint inventors may be named even if they did not physically work together, did not work at the same time, did not make the same type or amount of contribution, or did not make a contribution to the subject matter of every claim of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that joint inventors physically work together; one inventor can 'take a step at one time, the other an approach at different times.' However, two persons who had no contact and were completely unaware of each other's work cannot be joint inventors — some 'quantum of collaboration or connection' is required (e.g., collaboration, working under common direction, one inventor seeing a relevant report and building upon it, or hearing another's suggestion at a meeting). Cases: Monsanto Co. v. Kamp; Kimberly-Clark Corp. v. Procter & Gamble; Moler v. Purdy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution requirement for joint inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Each joint inventor generally must contribute to the conception of the invention, but need not make the same type or amount of contribution; partial contributions to the final solution are sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contribution to conception may be partial; differing roles or unequal contributions do not preclude joint inventorship if each makes some original contribution. Publication of a joint inventor's contribution before conception of the total invention does not necessarily defeat inventorship — partial contributions over time can be genuine contributions. Case examples: Monsanto Co. v. Kamp; Dana-Farber Cancer Inst. v. Ono Pharm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to a single claim suffices for inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint inventor need not contribute to every claim of a patent; a contribution to one claim is sufficient to be a joint inventor of that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: contributing a disclosed means for a means-plus-function claim element can make one a joint inventor as to that claim, unless the contributor only reduced to practice someone else's broader concept. Case: Ethicon Inc. v. United States Surgical Corp. There is no requirement that all inventors be joint inventors of the subject matter of any single claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries and correction of inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: When prosecution or amendments change who conceived the subject matter of remaining claims, examiners should inquire about inventorship and take steps for correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 602.09 regarding inquiries about inventorship of each claimed invention and correction of inventorship when applications are amended such that named inventors are no longer joint inventors of remaining claims. Also see MPEP § 602.01(c) et seq. for additional information on correction procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims given Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: During patent examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO construes claim scope not solely by claim language but by giving claims their broadest reasonable construction 'in light of the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.' This standard is applied by examiners during prosecution (distinct from how courts construe claims in litigation) to encourage applicant amendment and to establish a clear record. Relevant cases: Phillips v. AWH Corp.; In re American Academy of Science & Technology Center; In re Morris; In re Zletz.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI is not the broadest possible interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The BRI requirement does not permit the broadest possible interpretation; meanings must be consistent with ordinary and customary meaning and with the specification and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim term meanings must be what a person of ordinary skill would reasonably understand, taking into account any definitions or enlightenment in the written description. Examples: In re Cortright on 'restore hair growth'; Buszard on 'flexible' vs 'rigid' foam. Examiners should avoid overbroad readings inconsistent with the specification or skilled‑artisan understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain meaning under BRI: ordinary and customary meaning prevails
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, words of a claim must be given their plain (ordinary and customary) meaning unless that meaning is inconsistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain meaning is the meaning a person of ordinary skill in the art would give the term at the relevant time (effective filing date). Sources evidencing ordinary meaning include the claim language itself, the specification, drawings, and prior art; the specification is the best source. Cases include Phillips v. AWH Corp., Vitronics Corp. v. Conceptronic, and others. Example: simple English words are construed to mean exactly what they say absent contextual change (Chef America v. Lamb‑Weston).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from the specification into the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to read limitations from the specification (preferred embodiments) into the claims when the claim language is broader than the embodiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if only a single embodiment is described, the claims should not be limited to that embodiment absent a clear disclaimer. Courts have rejected importing unrecited limitations. However, when a claim element invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means‑plus‑function), the specification must be consulted to determine corresponding structure/material/acts, and the claim is limited to those and their equivalents. Cases: Superguide v. DirecTV; Liebel‑Flarsheim; E‑Pass; In re Donaldson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑plus‑function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: When an element is claimed under 112(f) (means‑/step‑plus‑function), the specification must be consulted to determine the structure, material, or acts corresponding to the function, and the element is construed as limited to that corresponding structure/material/acts and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim language falls under 112(f), examiners must identify corresponding disclosure in the specification to construe the limitation. See In re Donaldson and MPEP §§ 2181‑2186 for details and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extrinsic evidence in claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, dictionaries, treatises, etc.) may be consulted only when intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) does not offer sufficient clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification is the best source; when intrinsic evidence clearly supports an interpretation, extrinsic evidence is unnecessary. However, if intrinsic evidence is ambiguous or insufficient (e.g., unclear numeric boundaries), extrinsic evidence may be necessary to determine meaning to a person skilled in the art at the relevant time. Cases: Phillips; Actelion; Teva v. Sandoz; Seabed Geosolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant may act as lexicographer (special definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may rebut the presumption of ordinary meaning by clearly setting forth a special definition of a term in the specification that differs from its ordinary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To act as lexicographer, the definition must be presented with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision so that a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand the departure from common usage. The specification should clearly set out the uncommon definition. Cases: In re Paulsen; Intellicall; Toro Co. v. White Consolidated; Multiform Desiccants; Process Control Corp.; Apple v. Corephotonics. If an explicit definition is provided, that definition controls interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disavowal (disclaimer) of claim scope by applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may also rebut ordinary meaning by clearly and unmistakably disavowing or disclaiming the full scope of a claim term in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disavowal requires clear and unmistakable statements in the specification; in some cases disavowal may be made by implication (e.g., consistent disparagement of alternatives and exclusion in every embodiment). If an examiner believes BRI is narrower due to implicit disavowal, the examiner should make the interpretation clear on the record. Cases: SciMed Life Systems; In re American Academy of Sci. Tech. Ctr.; In re Abbott Diabetes Care. Note: prosecution history estoppel applies differently after issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowchart summary for claim term interpretation (non‑112(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural steps examiners should follow to ascertain claim interpretation for terms not invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1: Determine whether the claim term has an ordinary and customary meaning to those of ordinary skill. If yes, check the specification for a special definition. If no special definition, apply the ordinary meaning. If the specification provides a special definition, use it and the Office action should acknowledge and identify it. If the term lacks an ordinary meaning, check the specification for a meaning; if none, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation as best understood and consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of the preamble on claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a preamble limits a claim is determined case-by-case based on the entire claim; a preamble limits the claim if it is necessary to give life, meaning, and vitality to the claim or if the claim as a whole suggests limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no bright‑line test. Examiners should apply guideposts from case law (e.g., Catalina Marketing; Bell Communications; Pitney Bowes; Jansen) and consider whether the preamble recites limitations or is required to provide purpose/context that affects scope. Review facts of each case to decide whether the preamble limits the claim.
